FOR EACH NEW GUESS (an item of guesses, named G1, G2, ... as above): Before anything is built on this guess: first say what the cited records show about the result it starts from. Then name the earlier guess or hypothesis nearest to it. Then name the defect, or none. The defects: none: no defect; not_in_the_records: the result the guess starts from is not what the cited records show; repeats: the guess says again, in other words, what an earlier guess or hypothesis already said, and that one has its ruling; ignores_a_ruling: the guess goes on as if a ruling against it had not been given: it does not say what is different now; not_from_what_was_learned: the guess does not come from the newer records it cites: it would be the same guess without them; no_cause: the guess says that something makes no difference, or that nothing happens, without naming what in the system would make it so. A guess may be wrong and still be sound here: you judge whether it starts from what was measured and adds something, not whether it is true. A guess that takes up an earlier one with a stated difference (another cause, another range, a reason why the earlier test was not fair) is not a repetition. This is not the researcher's first guess, and a later guess has to be the fruit of what was learned since the earlier ones. The records marked NEW are what it says it learned from. Say in your reasoning what they show that the earlier guesses did not have, and ask: would the researcher have made this same guess without them? If yes, the citation is for form only and the defect is not_from_what_was_learned.

FOR EACH TEST (an item of tests, by its hypothesis): Before any of these simulations is run, answer three questions about this test, each with one sentence that cites record ids, then its box. Honest: can the test fail? Its result is not already known from the records, and its threshold is not one that almost any result passes. Consistent: does the rule test what the hypothesis claims, and only that? The simulations it compares differ only in what the claim is about, its measure can see it, and the competing guess explains the same result. Correct: say what the rule gives if the tested guess is true and the competing guess false, and what it gives if the competing guess is true and the tested guess false; pass only when the first is HELD and the second FAILED. Judge the competing guess the researcher named, do not replace it with your own. If the competing cause this test needs is a guess listed above other than the one the rule names, say so in feedback with its id; only if none of them states it, name it in missing. Last, feedback for the researcher: which question failed and the one problem that matters most, the record ids and numbers it rests on, and what a repaired test must achieve. The feedback never contains a decision rule, a measure@label, simulations or a network change: the researcher must find the repair itself. A test is not wanting for being small or for testing only one consequence of the guess.

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpCubic, TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpBbr, TcpVegas, TcpBic, default TcpCubic)
THE NETWORK MAY CHANGE TOO: in this brief a simulation may change the structure of the network (add or remove hosts, links, flows and queues; for example a link's queue replaced by a scheduler), as a legitimate way to test a guess; at most 2 hosts, 1 link, 2 flows; never removed: host:sender, flow:udp, link:l1, host:receiver. A planned simulation's change is shown with it (network changed: ...).
TOLERANCE: two results that differ by less than 1 % count as equal.

THE RESULT the guess is about: Scheduler q_full_time is 0.7s for Cubic/Bic, 0.1s for LinuxReno, and 0.0s for NewReno, while NewReno still has tcp_retrans=43.

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.

answer.because: E7 gives mean_tcp_cwnd=144773.920792 versus 126219.732673 and mean_q_tcp=89.306931 versus 77.079208, so C10's strict conjunction holds by margins far above 1%. Since the check held and the test was honest, consistent, and correct, the result is supported.

honest.why: C10 could have failed because E7's strict comparisons of mean_tcp_cwnd and mean_q_tcp were not fixed by E5/E6, and the observed gaps are not a threshold almost any result passes.

consistent.why: E7/C10 compare exactly the two mean quantities claimed by H10, with r011 and r010 differing only in tcp.type, while the competing guess explains the same q_full_time contrast by denying higher mean cwnd as the cause.

correct.why: C10 HELD because both E7 means are greater, which is what the tested guess predicts, whereas the competing guess as stated in the review predicts at least one mean comparison would not be greater.

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpCubic, TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpBbr, TcpVegas, TcpBic, default TcpCubic)
THE NETWORK MAY CHANGE TOO: in this brief a simulation may change the structure of the network (add or remove hosts, links, flows and queues; for example a link's queue replaced by a scheduler), as a legitimate way to test a guess; at most 2 hosts, 1 link, 2 flows; never removed: host:sender, flow:udp, link:l1, host:receiver. A planned simulation's change is shown with it (network changed: ...).
TOLERANCE: two results that differ by less than 1 % count as equal.

THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: UDP at 2 Gbps fills the sender-side FIFO queue, so TCP segments are tail-dropped before reaching the receiver.
  [Y2] guess: UDP offered load exceeds l1 capacity, so about half of UDP packets are dropped in the full queue.
  [Y3] guess: Receiver-side or TCP startup constraints prevent TCP delivery, so changing the sender queue will not help.
  [Y4] guess: A scheduler queue on l1 that gives each flow a share of the link will let TCP deliver nonzero goodput.
  [Y5] guess: The scheduler divides l1's byte service roughly equally between UDP and TCP, so TCP's 482 Mbps is its allocated share rather than a congestion-control result.
  [Y6] guess: TCP congestion control can increase TCP's share beyond the scheduler's equal share, for example by being more aggressive or delay-based.
  [Y7] guess: The large queue causes bufferbloat/timeouts that collapse TCP's usable window to about one segment, so a larger FIFO does not give TCP throughput.
  [Y8] guess: The new r002 record shows TCP is not merely receiver-window or handshake limited: it reaches tcp_cwnd_max=94120 and has tcp_retrans=18, yet remains at tcp_goodput_bps=5792, while r003's scheduler change raises TCP to tcp_goodput_bps=482007923; therefore q1000's residual TCP goodput is caused by queue-induced collapse/starvation under the queue service discipline, not by receiver-side or startup constraints.
  [Y9] guess: The back-direction utilization is TCP ACK traffic from receiver to sender, small enough that the receiver-side queue does not drop it.
  [Y10] guess: Bbr and Vegas keep TCP's scheduler queue underfilled, so UDP consumes the unused scheduler service.
  [Y11] guess: Cubic's larger cwnd oscillations overfill the TCP scheduler queue more often than NewReno's AIMD, causing more TCP drops at the same capped share.
  [Y12] guess: Increasing l1.queue.length under the scheduler lets TCP keep its queue nonempty and claim more of the allocated service, while decreasing it starves TCP.
  [Y13] guess: The full 1000-packet FIFO raises TCP's round-trip time enough to trigger RTO-driven collapse, leaving TCP sending only one or two segments per timeout; the scheduler with the same 1000-packet queue avoids that collapse, so the cause is FIFO queue-induced RTT/RTO rather than queue length alone.

  [Y17] guess: At the scheduler's capped share, the TCP congestion-control type's cwnd growth and oscillation determine how often the TCP scheduler queue overflows, so more aggressive types retransmit more without changing delivered goodput.
  [Y18] guess: Because the scheduler caps TCP goodput in these scheduler runs, the TCP queue's full time and drop count are set by queue capacity and class service rather than by TCP congestion-control type, so the retransmission differences among r003/r010/r011 are incidental.

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpCubic, TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpBbr, TcpVegas, TcpBic, default TcpCubic)

  [Y1] guess: UDP at 2 Gbps fills the sender-side FIFO queue, so TCP segments are tail-dropped before reaching the receiver.

  [Y3] guess: Receiver-side or TCP startup constraints prevent TCP delivery, so changing the sender queue will not help.
  [Y4] guess: A scheduler queue on l1 that gives each flow a share of the link will let TCP deliver nonzero goodput.
  [Y5] guess: The scheduler divides l1's byte service roughly equally between UDP and TCP, so TCP's 482 Mbps is its allocated share rather than a congestion-control result.
  [Y6] guess: TCP congestion control can increase TCP's share beyond the scheduler's equal share, for example by being more aggressive or delay-based.
  [Y7] guess: The large queue causes bufferbloat/timeouts that collapse TCP's usable window to about one segment, so a larger FIFO does not give TCP throughput.

  [Y10] guess: Bbr and Vegas keep TCP's scheduler queue underfilled, so UDP consumes the unused scheduler service.
  [Y11] guess: Cubic's larger cwnd oscillations overfill the TCP scheduler queue more often than NewReno's AIMD, causing more TCP drops at the same capped share.
  [Y12] guess: Increasing l1.queue.length under the scheduler lets TCP keep its queue nonempty and claim more of the allocated service, while decreasing it starves TCP.

  [Y1] (revised as Y7) UDP at 2 Gbps fills the sender-side FIFO queue, so TCP segments are tail-dropped before reaching the receiver.
  [Y2] UDP offered load exceeds l1 capacity, so about half of UDP packets are dropped in the full queue.
  [Y3] (refuted by V2) Receiver-side or TCP startup constraints prevent TCP delivery, so changing the sender queue will not help. | competes with Y1
  [Y4] (revised as Y5) A scheduler queue on l1 that gives each flow a share of the link will let TCP deliver nonzero goodput. | competes with Y3
  [Y5] The scheduler divides l1's byte service roughly equally between UDP and TCP, so TCP's 482 Mbps is its allocated share rather than a congestion-control result.
  [Y6] (refuted by V3) TCP congestion control can increase TCP's share beyond the scheduler's equal share, for example by being more aggressive or delay-based. | competes with Y5
  [Y7] (revised as Y13) The large queue causes bufferbloat/timeouts that collapse TCP's usable window to about one segment, so a larger FIFO does not give TCP throughput.
  [Y8] The new r002 record shows TCP is not merely receiver-window or handshake limited: it reaches tcp_cwnd_max=94120 and has tcp_retrans=18, yet remains at tcp_goodput_bps=5792, while r003's scheduler change raises TCP to tcp_goodput_bps=482007923; therefore q1000's residual TCP goodput is caused by queue-induced collapse/starvation under the queue service discipline, not by receiver-side or startup constraints.
  [Y9] The back-direction utilization is TCP ACK traffic from receiver to sender, small enough that the receiver-side queue does not drop it.
  [Y10] Bbr and Vegas keep TCP's scheduler queue underfilled, so UDP consumes the unused scheduler service. | competes with Y5
  [Y11] (revised as Y17) Cubic's larger cwnd oscillations overfill the TCP scheduler queue more often than NewReno's AIMD, causing more TCP drops at the same capped share. | competes with Y5
  [Y12] (refuted by V4) Increasing l1.queue.length under the scheduler lets TCP keep its queue nonempty and claim more of the allocated service, while decreasing it starves TCP. | competes with Y5
  [Y13] (revised as Y19) The full 1000-packet FIFO raises TCP's round-trip time enough to trigger RTO-driven collapse, leaving TCP sending only one or two segments per timeout; the scheduler with the same 1000-packet queue avoids that collapse, so the cause is FIFO queue-induced RTT/RTO rather than queue length alone.
  [Y14] (revised as Y20) The larger scheduler queue increases TCP queueing delay/RTT, so Cubic's effective rate falls slightly even though no TCP packets are dropped. | competes with Y5

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpCubic, TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpBbr, TcpVegas, TcpBic, default TcpCubic)

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpCubic, TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpBbr, TcpVegas, TcpBic, default TcpCubic)
THE NETWORK MAY CHANGE TOO: in this brief a simulation may change the structure of the network (add or remove hosts, links, flows and queues; for example a link's queue replaced by a scheduler), as a legitimate way to test a guess; at most 2 hosts, 1 link, 2 flows; never removed: host:sender, flow:udp, link:l1, host:receiver. A planned simulation's change is shown with it (network changed: ...).
